When can we let go of the inner solve?

PBGD-Free removes the value-function loop from a penalty method. The reason this can work is upper-level flatness—not simply using fewer updates.

Beyond Value Functions: Single-Loop Bilevel Optimization under Flatness Conditions

Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Lisha Chen, Tianyi Chen

The takeaway

PBGD-Free uses first-order updates without tracking the lower-level value function. Flatness conditions control the bias introduced by removing that correction.

01Explanation

When bilevel learning can skip a nested solve

One objective sits inside another

A bilevel learning problem has two roles. The lower-level problem learns a response for the current outer decision. The upper-level problem chooses the outer decision by evaluating that response. Even writing the problem is nested, so a straightforward solver often repeats many inner updates before making one outer update.

A penalty can still hide a solve

Penalty methods offer a first-order route: encourage the lower-level variable to reach a small objective gap. Yet evaluating that gap requires the lower-level optimum value. Maintaining the associated response introduces another stream of updates. The real question is which correction can be removed while controlling the resulting error.

01

Identify a flat upper objective

Bound how the upper loss changes when y moves away from a lower-level solution.

02

Drop the value-function loop

Use the simplified PBGD-Free update rather than estimating the full correction.

03

Control the remaining bias

Analyze convergence with the flatness parameters and the paper’s other assumptions.

The shortcut has a bias

PBGD-Free removes the value-function tracking component. Its lower-level variable takes gradient steps on a scaled penalty objective, while the upper-level variable follows the upper-level gradient. This is simpler, but the dropped term generally matters. The paper’s examples make that failure concrete rather than assuming that cheap updates must be correct.

Flatness gives the shortcut a regime

The flatness condition bounds how much the upper-level objective changes when the lower-level iterate moves away from a lower-level optimum. It includes an exponent, a modulus, and an additive allowance. These parameters help control the gap between the simplified update and the direction needed by the bilevel objective.

The structure comes before the speedup

The experiments study settings including LLM post-training, where a backbone and head play different optimization roles. The useful lesson is to look for a structural reason that a correction is small. Single-loop updates gain their justification from that structure and the convergence analysis. Their low per-iteration cost alone cannot provide it.

Removing a term creates a bias that must be explained

The full penalty gradient includes a correction involving the lower-level value function. Dropping it is attractive computationally, but it can leave a non-vanishing bias in a generic problem. Flatness supplies the additional structure used to bound the effect.

03Results

From a structural condition to LLM fine-tuning

Table 2 compares parameter-efficient fine-tuning of Llama-3-3B with a fixed training-time budget. The values below are the evaluated DPO loss at the trained outcome (xT, yT), not recognition errors or post-SFT results. The table reports no uncertainty for these values.

The experiments also study SFT loss, post-SFT outcomes, and flatness in the representation-learning formulation. These separate measurements help connect the proposed condition to the application without claiming it holds for every model or task.

Table 2 · First column, evaluated DPO loss in the paper

How to read this result

The simplified update is not a general recipe for every bilevel objective. Outside the analyzed flatness regime, the omitted correction can remain large and convergence can stop in a neighborhood of a stationary point.

The technical idea

The value-function correction is not automatically small

Two nearby lower-level responses do not by themselves imply a small penalty-gradient difference: that difference is multiplied by γ\gammaγ. This is why a large penalty alone cannot justify removing the correction.

Flatness measures upper-loss sensitivity

Definition 1 states |f(x, y⋆y^\stary⋆) − f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y)| ≤ c‖y⋆y^\stary⋆ − y‖^α\alphaα + δ\deltaδ. The residual δ\deltaδ permits local variation, while α\alphaα controls how the distance contribution shrinks near a lower-level optimum. The paper generally studies δ\deltaδ > 0 and α\alphaα > 1.

The simplified update still has a scope

The single-loop method alternates the lower-level update with an upper update based on ∇xf\nabla_x f∇x​f. Its analysis controls the omitted correction under flatness and the other assumptions. A flatness envelope by itself is not a convergence theorem.

The single-loop update

Lower update direction
dy,t=γ−1∇yf(xt,yt)+∇yg(xt,yt)\begin{aligned}d_{y,t}&=\gamma^{-1}\nabla_y f(x_t,y_t)\\&\quad+\nabla_y g(x_t,y_t)\end{aligned}dy,t​​=γ−1∇y​f(xt​,yt​)+∇y​g(xt​,yt​)​
One lower-level step
yt+1=yt−ηγ dy,ty_{t+1}=y_t-\eta_\gamma\,d_{y,t}yt+1​=yt​−ηγ​dy,t​
One upper-level step
xt+1=xt−η dx,tdx,t=∇xf(xt,yt+1)\begin{aligned}x_{t+1}&=x_t-\eta\,d_{x,t}\\d_{x,t}&=\nabla_x f(x_t,y_{t+1})\end{aligned}xt+1​dx,t​​=xt​−ηdx,t​=∇x​f(xt​,yt+1​)​

Algorithm 1, with the common choice K=1K=1K=1: update the lower variable, then use the updated lower iterate for the upper step. ηγ\eta_\gammaηγ​ and η are the lower and upper step sizes. The missing value-function correction is precisely what the flatness analysis must account for.

Assumptions and guarantee

The convergence analysis combines smoothness, lower-level PL-type conditions, the flatness parameters, and algorithmic step-size choices. It quantifies stationarity error and the bias from omitting the value-function term. See Definition 1 and the convergence results in Section 3.
